desc: The beat-band sound that emerged in the early 1960s from the club scene around Liverpool's River Mersey. The Beatles are its best-known exponents, and it laid the groundwork for the British Invasion.

The phenomenon, around 1964, in which British bands led by the Beatles swept the American charts one after another. It kicked off a two-way musical exchange between the UK and US that continued for decades.
A 1960s British youth subculture defined by sharp suits and scooters, favoring bands influenced by R&B and soul (such as The Who).

term: NWOBHM (New Wave of British Heavy Metal)
desc: A young, aggressive generation of heavy metal that emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s, partly influenced by punk. Iron Maiden and Judas Priest are its leading names.

The name of a cassette compilation distributed by the British music magazine NME in 1986. The term also came to describe the raw, noisy, low-budget guitar pop it captured, and it became one wellspring of later indie rock.
A movement from the late 1980s to early 1990s, centered on Manchester's Haçienda club, that fused rock with dance music and acid house. The Stone Roses and Happy Mondays are its leading names.
A guitar-rock movement of the mid-1990s that strongly foregrounded British identity, fueled in large part by the rivalry between Oasis and Blur (the so-called "Britpop Wars").

A genre marked by thick walls of guitar noise and effects paired with floating, ethereal vocals. It was named for musicians who spent performances staring down at their effects pedals — "gazing" at their "shoes."
A movement from the late 1970s to the 1980s that carried forward punk's DIY spirit while pursuing more experimental, introspective music. Joy Division is a leading example.

An umbrella term for music after post-punk that actively embraced synthesizers and a pop sensibility. It refers less to a single genre than to the broader experimental, modern current that followed punk.
A genre branching off from post-punk, marked by a dark, aestheticized worldview. It also developed into a visual subculture defined by black clothing and makeup.
A genre from the early 1970s combining flamboyant makeup and costumes with addictively poppy rock sounds. David Bowie and T. Rex are its defining figures.
1970s rock that drew on classical and jazz vocabulary in pursuit of long, complex song structures. King Crimson and Yes are its leading names; often shortened to "prog."

A mid-1970s current that reacted against increasingly commercial, large-scale rock by favoring stripped-down, honest performances in small venues like pubs. It is often positioned as a precursor to punk.
A club that opened in Manchester in 1982. It became the epicenter of Madchester and acid house, and played a major role in fusing British club culture with rock.
